Sports.title: Shane Lowry secures incredible piece of Masters history as Irishman stuns fans with latest Augusta hole-in-one
Sports.content:
Shane Lowry has become the first golfer in history to get multiple holes-in-one at the Masters.

The beloved Irishman delighted the patrons at Augusta National on Saturday afternoon as aced the 190-yard, par-3 sixth hole early in his third round.

It catapulted him to within four of the lead held by close friend Rory McIlroy, who saw his commanding position wilt away early on Saturday.

Lowry's shot pitched below the hole and taken a couple of bounces before rolling in for only the seventh ace at that hole in the tournament’s history.

The moment sparked wild celebrations on the course and Lowry's playing partner, Tommy Fleetwood, embraced his Ryder Cup teammate.

The shot was so good that even American player Harris English paused and pretended to bow down to Lowry on the nearby 16th green.

Shane Lowry has become the first golfer in history to get multiple holes-in-one at the Masters

The moment sparked wild celebrations among fans and with playing partner Tommy Fleetwood

It was just the 35th time a hole-in-one has been scored at the Masters and now Lowry has two

Needing one stroke on No. 6, Shane Lowry cards an ace. #themasters pic.twitter.com/SAr9uy2KBs — The Masters (@TheMasters) April 11, 2026

It was just the 35th time a hole-in-one has been scored at the Masters and now Lowry has two of them.

His previous hole-in-one here came at the 16th in the final round of 2016. It was also his second ace in a month after recording one at March’s Texas Children’s Houston Open.

Lowry has also aced the 17th at Sawgrass, in 2022, and the short seventh at Pebble Beach, in January 2025, two of the most famous par threes in golf.

Thanks to his latest effort on Saturday, Lowry will be awarded a large crystal bowl as a prize by Augusta National.

Sports.title: Rory McIlroy spills on his unconventional Masters prep - involving a $50m private jet and 'dinners with wife Erica'
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy spills on his unconventional Masters prep - involving a $50m private jet and 'dinners with wife Erica'

Rory McIlroy has revealed the secret behind his dominant form at the 2026 Masters.

The defending champion has been making use of his $50million (£38m) private jet to fly back and forth to Augusta National for extra practice sessions on the course.

While most golfers hunker down in Georgia for the week, McIlroy is opting to fly back to his Florida mansion every evening to maintain his routine.

The Northern Irishman revealed that the strategy allows him to stay connected to his family, specifically his wife Erica Stoll and daughter Poppy.

He said: 'I honestly just don't like the three tournaments leading up to this event. I'd rather come up here. I did a couple of days where I dropped Poppy to school.

'Then flew up here, played, landed back home and had dinner with her or had dinner with Erica.'

Rory McIlroy stormed into the largest halfway lead in Masters history at Augusta on Friday

McIlroy and Stoll also made sure to pose for a picture alongside their daughter, Poppy

The 530-mile trek from his home in Jupiter, Florida, to the hallowed grounds of Augusta typically takes around two hours each way in the air.

Despite the travel time, McIlroy believes the mental benefits of sleeping in his own bed far outweigh the exhaustion of a cross-state commute.

The star, who is currently seeking to become the first player since Tiger Woods to win back-to-back Green Jackets, is clearly in a relaxed headspace.

His preparation is paying off on the scorecard, with McIlroy sitting at an astonishing 12-under par following a clinical second-round performance.

The luxury jet, which he purchased in late 2024, can sit up to 19 passengers and features plush sofas designed for maximum comfort and legroom.

However, the convenience comes with a staggering price tag, with reports suggesting the aircraft costs roughly $4,000 (£3,000) per hour to operate.

A single day of practice - including four hours of total flight time - can rack up bills of up to $16,000 (£12,000) for the world’s most famous active golfer.

Beyond the financial cost, the trips have drawn some scrutiny regarding the environmental impact of such frequent, short-term private aviation.

Four hours of flying time in a private jet can produce up to eight to 16 metric tonnes of CO2.

Dozens of private jets had already arrived at Augusta Regional Airport by Monday afternoon

Before the action began at the Masters, PrivateJet.com director of charter sales, Michael Loff, gave the Daily Mail a glimpse of how the other half live.

He explained that many visitors asked for planes with enough space to fit their own clubs. Such as the King Air 350, which comes with wing lockers originally designed for skis. On one of those, it's barely a two-hour trip from Palm Beach or the South Carolina paradise of Hilton Head.

And yet? Take a King Air 350 to and from the Masters and it will set you back around $15-18,000. A bigger jet comes with a bigger price tag of $30,000 plus.



Parking spots are at a premium and at major sporting events - such as the Masters or the Super Bowl - airports will slap on 'special event fees'. At Augusta airport this week, they range from $150 to $4,000, depending on the aircraft's size.

Sports.title: Jon Rahm is a pale impression of the golfing titan he once was as Spaniard's dismal Masters performance shows his prime years are passing him by
Sports.content:
AN observation about Jon Rahm: when this wounded Spaniard gets angry with himself, which is increasingly often, he tends to swear in English. Confusing as that might seem, it is about right for a man who appears so at odds with himself.

Because what is he these days? Is he one of the very best in the game? Probably, yes. But is he even close to what he was or might have been?

That is a more complicated question, answered by a series of desperately underwhelming numbers on his scorecards this week at the Masters.

And so he trundled around his third round at Augusta National, a little out of place among the early cohort of starters, which is a politer way of saying Rahm was an also-ran.

Naturally, there are those departed from here who would be thrilled to make the cut, and he made it bang on the number, but Rahm, Rahmbo, was the pre-tournament favourite. More than that, he was the 2023 champion, a titan of the Ryder Cup, and for 52 weeks he was the world's top-ranked player.

But he hasn't looked much like that guy here and he was a pale impression again on Saturday.

The feared Spaniard known as 'Rhambo' is hardly the threat he once was a few years ago

He had spoken after his first-round 78 of needing a 'miracle' and followed his 70 a day later by admitting only a 'heck of a round' might save his week. Finishing a full hour before Rory McIlroy even began, he carded a 73; in other words, he went backwards and it is hard to shake the urge to think the same of his career in general since joining LIV in late 2023.

Can the pocketing of £400million ever be rated a mistake? Well, that's an old debate and one that boils down to priorities, but at 31, we are forever acquiring new evidence to suggest his prime years are passing him by. That his relevance among the cream has diminished into a series of nostalgia-based predictions and reality-check results on the biggest stages.

We should add that Rahm has not become a bad golfer by any stretch – his major finishes since the end of 2023 read: T45, cut, injured, T7, T14, T8, T7, T34, plus whatever he delivers on Sunday, which will most likely be deep into double digits. Objectively, that is a good body of work, but everything is relative.

Back in 2021, for instance, when Rahm won the US Open, he was never lower than eighth in a major, and in his final season as a PGA Tour player, in 2023, he not only won the Masters but also finished second at the Open and 10th at the US Open. That was his level, supported by 17 other titles between 2017 and 2023 on the DP World Tour and PGA Tour.

Rahm is seen reacting on the seventh green during the third round at Augusta National

Regrettably, the slide is unmistakeable from a player who was expected to spend an entire era in battle with McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler.

He can perform in the smaller fields and gentler courses of LIV, where he has been excellent in 2026, but iron sharpens irons and there are too many blunt, faded stars on his day-to-day tour.

Ask him about that and he'll deny it, of course, as he did rather tetchily on Friday. Just as he has previously denied the oft-repeated rumour of 'buyer's remorse' since moving. Tyrrell Hatton, his LIV team-mate, told me last year that those assumptions are little more than 'media bull****' but many folk of importance in golf believe it to be true.

One senior figure on the DP World Tour told me as much earlier this week under the grand oak tree outside the Augusta clubhouse. It's where the great and good here mingle and do deals and Rahm's agent has been there most days – it is tempting to wonder if Rahm has ever queried to him privately if they were right to sign the biggest one of all.

We have seen Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed quit LIV in the past few months and there is no certainty whatsoever that Bryson DeChambeau will get the $500million he is apparently requesting to stay beyond this year.

If he goes, where does that leave LIV? And where does it leave Rahm, having gone all-in on this concept and whose contract is understood to run through 2027? For now, we are seeing a golfer in no-man's land and stubbornly committed to a nonsensical row with the DP World Tour over unpaid fines. A place in the next Ryder Cup, the final domain where his stock is enormous, remains in peril if he does not back down.

We tried to discuss that with him earlier in the week and met a minor protestation that he was here to talk about the Masters. The place where many of us, myself included, tipped him to win. But he did let a few thoughts slip and offered an assurance he will be at Adare Manor in 2027, albeit to some surprise from the Tour with whom he is currently squabbling.

Rahm plays a shot on the eighth hole during the third round of the 2026 Masters Tournament

To watch him play golf is still to get reminders that he can play shots like few others. Also that he is a massive draw to galleries wherever he competes.

But this third round was sad and summed up somewhat by his final hole, where for the third time in a handful of hours he shouted 'fore right' off the tee before playing his next shot from an awkward stance under a bush. There was magic in the pitch over sand that gave him an eight-footer to save par and there was an inevitability that he then missed the putt.

That, sadly, has been the story of his week and much of the past three years.

When he wrapped up, he had little to say. 'I came in with the same expectations I come into any other major, any other tournament - not any higher or lower,' he said. 'If I knew the why, two things: I'm probably not going to say it right now, and I would have tried to avoid it if I knew.'

He sounded confused. As are all the onlookers who swear by memories of what he could do in the not-so-distant past.

Sports.title: Oxlade-Chamberlain provides the star quality as Celtic grind out win over St Mirren to keep their title hopes alive
Sports.content:
Celtic 1 St Mirren 0

On a day when anything less than all three points was simply unthinkable from a Celtic perspective, Martin O’Neill’s players scrambled their way to a victory which keeps their title defence alive.

We are very much at the stage of the season where results matter more than performances - which is just as well for a team who remain wholly unconvincing.

On the balance of play, they just about deserved the win here but were made to sweat and toil for it by a progressive and well organised St Mirren side who strained every sinew in their own bid to avoid the relegation play-off spot.

Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain’s early goal might have been expected to provide Celtic with a platform for a more comfortable afternoon.

Instead, they retreated into a shell at times, especially during a spell of the second half when St Mirren looked the likelier side but without asking any serious questions of home keeper Viljami Sinisalo.

Oxlade-Chamberlain celebrates after scoring early in the 1-0 win over St Mirren

It remains difficult to envisage this Celtic side putting together a run of five straight wins when the post split fixtures commence in a fortnight, even if three of their games are at home.

Yet they are still in there pitching and have a degree of tenacity under O’Neill which means they remain contenders for a Premiership and Scottish Cup double.

To win the latter, they will need to overcome St Mirren again at Hampden next Sunday and that is no foregone conclusion.

Interim Saints boss Craig McLeish oversaw another admirable display from his players here which will give him belief they can steer clear of that dreaded 11th place in the table. They are now just two points clear of Kilmarnock but look to have enough to survive.

Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain keeps his cool to put Celtic 1-0 up against St MIrren

Celtic’s decision to welcome the unrepentant Green Brigade back to the stadium, with the ultras group even demanding an apology from the club in response to the news their five month ban was being lifted, was perhaps an exercise in pragmatism by the board of directors.

You would certainly have given a penny for chairman Brian Wilson’s thoughts when the returning section of the support unfurled a banner before kick-off with a quote from IRA hunger striker Bobby Sands’ prison diaries - ‘Everyone has their own particular part to play’.

Whatever the politics of the situation, there was certainly a more buoyant and noisy atmosphere inside Celtic Park as the defending champions sought to build a sense of unity on and off the pitch for the title run-in.

Oxlade-Chamberlain hasn’t made as much of an impact as O’Neill might have hoped when he recruited the former Liverpool and Arsenal man as a free agent in February but the 32-year-old still possesses smatterings of star quality.

Tomas Cvancara catches St Mirren goalkeeper Shamal George on the head

Before he put Celtic in front, Oxlade-Chamberlain had already displayed his technical prowess with a sweetly struck volley beyond Shamal George after the St Mirren keeper had parried a long range shot from Callum McGregor.

That effort was quickly and correctly ruled out for offside but there was no dispute over his 16th minute breakthrough which came in similar circumstances.

St Mirren had actually settled into the game after a difficult start but were undone when another McGregor shot was blocked by Alex Gogic whose fellow defenders were slow to react to the loose ball.

Oxlade-Chamberlain was onto it like a flash and whipped an emphatic low finish beyond the helpless George.

If the home fans expected an onslaught to follow, they were disappointed. While Celtic dominated possession, St Mirren dug in and kept the ball with good composure whenever it came their way.

Mikael Mandron should have done better than head wide from a Miguel Freckleton cross as the visitors indicated they would carry a threat of their own.

They suffered a blow, however, in the 32nd minute when George was hurt in a painful clash with Tomas Cvancara as he bravely challenged the big Czech striker who was trying to get on the end of Daizen Maeda’s low ball across the face of the six yard box. George was unable to continue after lengthy treatment and was replaced by former Celtic youth player Ryan Mullen.

Celtic striker Kelechi Iheanacho misses a chance to make the result safe

St Mirren’s deputy, making only his second league appearance for the club, enjoyed an early confidence boost when he did well to clutch a curling shot from Celtic’s top scorer Benjamin Nygren.

Celtic looked increasingly nervy as the first half ticked into six minutes of stoppage time and Liam Donnelly almost grabbed a leveller for Saints when he headed narrowly over from Declan John’s corner.

The anxiety levels continued to escalate for the hosts after the break. There was a lack of fluidity in their work while St Mirren grew in confidence and ambition, albeit without being able to create clear cut openings.

Cvancara had yet again delivered a wholly underwhelming display up front for Celtic and the Borussia Moenchengladbach loanee was replaced by Kelechi Iheanacho for the final half hour.

St Mirren interim manager Craig McLeish looks on from the sidelines during Saturday's game

The Nigerian’s fitness issues make his inability to play the full 90 minutes another source of concern for O’Neill who has already conceded that Celtic’s striking problems mean they have no chance of winning the title on goal difference if it comes down to it.

Iheanacho did show he could still have a crucial role to play when he came off the bench to grab the winner at Dundee last Sunday and the former Manchester City man had an opportunity to ease the tension for Celtic here.

He was picked out by Maeda’s low cross from the left but miscued his near post effort and sent it wide from inside the six yard box.

Celtic ultimately saw the game out and proceeded on a lap of honour to acknowledge their supporters.

As they reached the Green Brigade section, new banners were unfurled reading ‘Celtic Board - Unfit For Purpose’ and ‘Unbowed, Unbroken’.

Unity, it seems, is still very much a fragile concept at Celtic Park.

Sports.title: Zack Polanski is trying to fool the country into banning racing. But the Grand National proved why he must be stopped from blowing a £4.1bn hole in the economy, writes DOMINIC KING
Sports.content:
There is a world that Zack Polanski envisages in which none of this would have occurred. No joy, no history, no opportunity to say 'I was there'.

Mr Polanski, the leader of the Green Party, would abolish horseracing if he had the opportunity. He’s a politician, evidently, that is adept at saying things to capture a headline but equally evident is his lack of knowledge about what a crucial role this industry plays in the country. Don’t let him fool you.

It is at this time of year when a lot of people like to shout and scream about the Randox Grand National, the kind of people you get the sense are hoping for a calamity to unfold so they can screech: 'we told you so!'

But here’s the thing – Aintree is growing in popularity, as is horseracing as a whole as attendances continue to climb. A sell-out 60,000 crowd braved horrible conditions yesterday and the figure for the last three days was more than 141,000, the biggest since 2018.

That is hugely significant, as racing really suffered after the pandemic. It was never going to be like football, where tribalism and long-standing loyalties meant fans would always flock back to the clubs once they had permission. Racing, by contrast, had a challenge to hold on to its customers.

Polanski is a long-standing critic of all forms of racing, saying on social media in 2024 that the Aintree showpiece combined 'gambling and animal cruelty'

But those charged with driving the industry forward are constantly looking to improve, to make it as safe as possible and ensure it is governed properly and with integrity

Opportunists such as Polanski and campaign groups have seized on incidents and the awful situation that befell Gold Dancer on Friday, when he suffered a fatal injury, enabled critics to charge in headfirst and blast inflammatory comments.

Everyone is entitled to their view but it doesn’t help when people don’t arm themselves with facts and figures or listen to experts give detailed analysis of situations. What happens, for instance, to the 20,000 thoroughbreds in the United Kingdom if Polanski abolished racing?

Where do the 85,000 people in the industry, many of whom are on primitive wages, find alternative employment? What fills the £4.1billion hole that would be left in the country’s economy if the sport ceased to exist?

Racing isn’t perfect and there are issues to address. But those charged with driving the industry forward are constantly looking to improve, to make it as safe as possible and ensure it is governed properly and with integrity.

We can never guarantee 100 per cent safety in a race or with anything to do with livestock but what we can guarantee is that racing continues to grip the nation; whether it is Aintree or a provincial track such as Newton Abbot, who last week welcomed a record 8500 crowd, it is captivating.

Paul Hayward, a doyen of sports journalists, once called the thoroughbred 'the monarch of the animal kingdom' and it is a beautiful phrase. Its majesty must be allowed to flourish.

Sports.title: Who would avoid tax in a house like this? The £5million Isle of Man mansion that could save Tyson Fury handing Rachel Reeves his millions
Sports.content:
Who would avoid tax in a house like this? The £5million Isle of Man mansion that could save Tyson Fury handing Rachel Reeves his millions

Have YOU got a story? Email tips@dailymail.co.uk

This is the lavish £5million mansion on the Isle of Man where Tyson Fury has moved his family - to become a tax exile in the middle of the Irish Sea.

The two-time heavyweight boxing champion - who fights again tonight - officially relocated to this 200-year-old country manor house last December.

Their new nine-acre Isle of Man estate, revealed here for the first time, is perched on a hill with expansive views of the surrounding countryside close to the pretty harbour town of Peel.

The three-storey property - approached by a long private gated drive winding through mature woodland and formal gardens - boasts four reception areas, six bedrooms, five bathrooms, a study and leisure area with a cinema room, gymnasium, games room and sauna.

There is also a fully renovated two bedroom coach house on site as well as a garage block and a stone-built paddock with stables for four horses and a tack room.

Tyson, his wife Paris and their seven children have been enjoying their new life on the island popping to a harbour-side pub for cozy fish and chip lunches and treating his children to Italian gelato ice creams by the sea.

Tyson, who has come out of retirement to fight Arslanbek Makhmudov at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium tonight, has kept in shape by jogging along a picturesque former railway line, which stretches ten miles between Peel and the island's capital Douglas.

And the Daily Mail can also reveal Tyson, 37, and wife Paris, 36, are also understood to have booked a luxury hotel and resort less than ten miles from their new home for their daughter Venezuela's wedding next month.

Revealed: The lavish £5million mansion where boxer Tyson Fury moved his family last December

The 200-year-old country manor, part of a nine-acre estate, is located on the Isle of Man

The Furys with six of their seven children as part of a promotion for the Netflix series At Home With The Furys

Tyson celebrates victory with his wife Paris after the WBC World Heavyweight Title Fight against Dillian Whyte at Wembley Stadium on April 23, 2022

But there's another reason other than tourist attractions for their move here from their previous base in Morecambe on the Lancashire coast: tax.

The Isle of Man offers a top income tax rate of 21 per cent and a tax cap of £220,000, far lower than the 40-45 per cent he was paying previously on the mainland.

There is also no capital gains tax, inheritance tax, wealth tax or stamp duty.

Fury is worth around £200million. His company's last report showed he had a fortune of £162million in 2024, but this has risen considerably since.

Fury is expected to pocket £18.8million for his fight fee against Makhmudov and around £6million in endorsements from sponsors including broker XTB and Swedish tech game company Boxbollen.

Then adding revenue from his own drinks brand Furocity and selling merchandise via his website, Fury is set to bring his total annual earnings this year to around £25million.

He is likely to be paying the Isle of Man tax cap of just £220,000 which can be capped at that amount for up to ten years - whereas if he were paying tax in the UK the bill would be closer to £11.25million.

It means Tyson is likely to save around £11million on his earnings this year by moving - and that even after spending £5million on the house he is still better off by some £6million.

And the amount he saves in a single night on tax tonight - which would otherwise be payable on that £18.8million fee for fighting - could be in the region of £8-9million.

The Furys had previously lived in a beachfront house in Morecambe for over a decade but decided to leave for financial reasons.

Fury has never made any secret about his frustration at his tax burden in the mainland UK.

In 2023 speaking to iFL TV, the heavyweight superstar claimed: ‘Here's an interesting fact, I pay more tax than the whole of Morecambe combined… There's probably about about 20,000 people.’

The 'Gipsy King' - director of his firm Tyson Fury Ltd - changed his residency status with Companies House at the end of last year to the Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency which imposes no capital gains or inheritance taxes.

Paris, who has done the same on her business documents, last week told the Daily Mail that the decision to move was made by her husband just before Christmas - a month after Chancellor Rachel Reeves slapped a new tax on mansions worth over £2million in her budget.

She said: 'This has gone on for years, the thought process of moving away. And then it was, "Boom, we're going."

'That's Tyson all over. But you know, we are travellers by heritage, so it's not as strange to us [to move about] as it may be to others.'

Paris quickly became the practical one in their partnership: at just 18, while still on their honeymoon, it was she who scrutinised her new husband's first professional contract

The three-storey property boasts four reception areas, six bedrooms, five bathrooms, a study and leisure area with a cinema room, gymnasium, games room and sauna

They were also forced to move from the luxury Lancashire mansion amid security concerns, after several overzealous fans turned up at the family's door.

Tyson revealed ahead of tonight's fight the Furys had been the victims of several stalking incidents during their time at the £1.7million property.

He had to disconnect the intercom after a series 'crackpots and drunk people' rang asking to speak with him - and now has an attack dog for protection.

On one occasion, police had to be called after a man in a dressing gown and pyjamas scaled the some 40-foot gates and asked to be adopted by the family.

And in another bizarre instance, a man wearing seashells from head to toe turned up at the house, saying God had spent him to speak with Tyson.

'I've had a million nut jobs at my place,' the fighter said.

At 6ft 9in Tyson cuts a larger than life character on the island but he tries to lead as normal a life as possible despite this.

He was spotted shopping in Tesco earlier this year, with one onlooker joking: 'You couldn't miss him as he towered over everyone. But luckily people weren't bothering him.'

The Manchester United fan was accosted by players from the local Peel FC who spotted him walking past the front of the Peveril Hotel and persuaded him to pose for a selfie with them.

His pub of choice, however, is The Creek Inn on Peel quayside, where he often feasts on fish and chips.

A waitress at the Victorian pub said: 'I haven't seen him myself but he's been in a few times for lunch, usually on his own. He's very friendly apparently and always obliges people when they want a photo with him.'

Pradeep Rawat, owner of The Boatyard seafood restaurant in Peel, joked how he turfed Tyson out last year when he was scoping properties on the island.

He said: 'I didn't know it was Tyson Fury at the time. This really tall guy came in and asked if he could have a table but I had to turn him away because it was during the TT Races, which is such a chaotic time, and we were so busy.

'He was very good about it and was really polite. It was only afterwards that I realised who he was. I get teased now that I threw out the heavyweight champ.

'But of course Tyson and his family are always welcome. We'll be cheering him on.'

The doting father has been seen treating his children to ice cream at Gelatory in Peel. As has his brother, Tommy, who is rumoured to be house hunting on the Isle of Man with influencer fiancee Molly Mae.

Tyson also takes 15-year-old son Prince to a boxing gym in Douglas and recently posed for a selfie with Rachel Marsland, co-owner of jacket potato takeaway Terry's Tatos in the town.

Rachel said: 'He was a lovely bloke, really humble, really funny. He helped me clear up and everything.'

Paris Fury, 36, gave fans a glimpse into the family's new six-bedroom home on the tax haven of the Isle of Man, that is said to have cost £5million

Tyson and Paris have been together since they were teenagers and got married in Doncaster, South Yorkshire, in 2008

Meanwhile, two weeks ago Paris took the children to the Barbary West Coast pub and restaurant on the outskirts of Peel for dinner.

Barman Ben Davies, 19, said: 'Paris asked if we did karaoke, she said that she was looking for somewhere she and the kids could sing.

'We don't do karaoke unfortunately but they ended up having a few soft drinks, playing pool and having a bit of a dance by the bar.

'They were a really nice down-to-earth family.

The Furys travel back to the mainland regularly, usually aboard the three-hour 45-minute ferry crossing between Douglas and Heysham in Lancashire, a 15-minute drive from their other home in Morecambe.

While Tyson has been training in Thailand for the last three months, Paris and Venezuela took the rest of the family to London this week to promote the second series of their fly-on-the-wall Netflix show At Home With The Furys, which airs tomorrow (Sunday).

Paris uploaded videos onto her Instagram page showing her and the children enjoying a visit to the Mundo Pixar Experience in Wembley, north London before going to watch Disney's Hercules at the Theatre Royal Drury Lane.

Tyson and Paris have been together since they were teenagers and were first married in 2008 at St Peter in Chains Catholic Church in Doncaster, South Yorkshire, when he was 21 and she was just 19.

They have renewed their vows twice since, in New York and then Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur in the South of France.

Now, despite still being just 16, their eldest child, Venezuela is soon to marry too - she's engaged to 17-year-old aspiring boxer Noah Price.

Her hen party was held back in Morecambe but the rumour on the Isle of Man, is that the Furys have hired The Comis Hotel and Resort on the outskirts of Douglas for their daughter's upcoming wedding.

A source said: 'The Comis which is probably the fanciest place to get married on the Isle of Man.

Pictured: Valencia Amber, Prince Tyson Fury II, Prince John James, Paris, Athena, Tyson, Prince Adonis Amaziah and Venezuela in season two of the family's Netflix show At Home With The Furys

'It's a very elegant location and because it's away from the mainland and surrounded by 250-acres of countryside they're probably away from the glare of publicity. They'll have a degree of privacy here. It's the talk of the island at the moment.'

Meanwhile the family's new country pile sits beneath Slieau Whallian, a 900ft high steep hill where, according to local legend, women accused of being witches were once put into a barrel, with sharp iron spikes inserted inwards, and rolled down from the summit.

On stormy nights, the screams of the 'witches' can still be heard rushing through the trees, so the local folk legend goes.



Fans will be hoping that Tyson is screaming with delight at the end of this evening's bout.

Sports.title: Leinster 43-13 Sale: The Sharks' European dream may be dead - but here's why there are better days ahead despite a disappointing season, writes ALEX BYWATER
Sports.content:
In the build-up to this game, Sale boss Alex Sanderson told Daily Mail Sport of his desire to put his team back on the global rugby map through the strength of their performances.

The Sharks have had a tough season, winning just three PREM Rugby games. And while this was another defeat which ended their European hopes, elements of their display – particularly the first half – showed what the Manchester-based club can do. Maybe, in time, Sanderson will get his wish.

Sale hassled and harried Leinster on occasion who, despite the nature of the final score, seem to be a shadow of their former selves. Leo Cullen’s side were particularly poor in the first 40. Leaving Dublin, you had to wonder what Sanderson’s men could have done if they’d had their England stars Tom and Ben Curry, Luke Cowan-Dickie, Bevan Rodd and Raffi Quirke available. All were absent here due to injury.

Two yellow cards suffered by the Sharks were also crucial as at one point they were down to 13 men. Leinster will now host Toulon back in Dublin in the Champions Cup’s last four.

The Irish giants haven’t won this competition since 2018 and are placing a significant emphasis on ending that run this season.

But on the evidence of this showing, they will not be able to trouble teams such as Bath or Bordeaux and Toulouse who meet on Sunday.

Sale Sharks are out of the Champions Cup after a 43-13 defeat by Leinster in the quarter-finals - but boss Alex Sanderson can take hope from this performance

Sale harried and hassled Leinster and Sanderson said his team can use the showing as fuel

Leinster have called Aviva Stadium their home this season due to redevelopments at the RDS Arena down the road. But the attendance of 18,839 at the home of Irish rugby was particularly underwhelming. It gave what was on paper a huge European quarter-final the feeling of a pre-season friendly. Only the Aviva’s lower tier was open to supporters.

Protests in Dublin and across Ireland at the price of fuel and subsequent road closures may have played a part.

Without their two first-choice hookers, the task facing Sale was tough. They fell behind to a score from Leinster’s Irish try machine and hooker Dan Sheehan. As usual, Sheehan was a force of nature, even appearing in the back-row late on. But the flat-as-a-pancake atmosphere seemed to hinder Leinster and, conversely, aid Sale.

George Ford put boot to ball on almost every occasion, with conditions being worsened by pre-match rain. It was not a pretty spectacle. But it was also exactly what Sale wanted to ensure they stayed in the contest. Leinster were never really under threat, but they also made mistake after mistake. Sale must take some credit for that.

Their scrum was impressive and when Leinster’s Joe McCarthy was penalised, Ford put the visitors on the board.

To that point, Sale’s plan was working well. But four minutes before the break, Dan du Preez went to intercept a Jamison Gibson-Park pass and was yellow carded for a deliberate knock on. Still, Sale went to the break only four behind, with Ford putting a drop goal effort wide.

One thing not going Sale’s way was their line-out which struggled badly and after a strong first period, things unravelled for the Sharks when the second half began. Hugo Keenan crossed for Leinster’s second, though the ball looked to have gone forward in the build-up. To add salt to the wound, prop Si McIntyre followed Du Preez to the sin bin for a high tackle.

Ford responded with a long-range penalty with Du Preez then returning to the field.

Leinster are into the semi-finals but they do not look like winning the competition for the first time since 2018

This tie felt like a pre-season friendly due to the low attendance and poor atmosphere

Rekeiti Ma'asi-White led Sale’s display with a powerful midfield display, but Leinster’s third and fourth scores – which came through Ryan Baird and Rieko Ioane respectively – put the game to bed. Sale, wounded by fitness troubles and subsequently lacking strength in depth, ran out of puff in the final quarter. Tommy O’Brien made it five from a wicked bounce.

MATCH FACTS Leinster scorers Tries: Sheehan, Keenan, Baird, Ioane, O’Brien, Osborne Cons: Byrne (5) Pen: Byrne Sale Sharks scorers Try: Wills Con: Ford Pens: Ford (2) Referee: Pierre Brousset (France) Star man: Dan Sheehan (Leinster)

It was harsh on Sale and flattered Leinster no end, not that those in the Aviva seemed particularly bothered. The whole game, in truth, felt underwhelming due to the poor atmosphere and low crowd. There was barely a murmur when Sale replacement Alex Wills finished in the corner for a late but deserved consolation.

Sheehan set-up Jamie Osborne to complete the job for Leinster late on.

'Leinster are too good to give that many opportunities. Not winning your own ball is one of the things you can control,' Sanderson reflected.

‘There are only so many times Leinster can huff and puff before they blow the door down. I don’t believe the score was reflective of the effort the boys put in or the nature of the game. We want more of this.

‘We want to get into Europe again. There’s always the motivation to want to improve. Clearly, we’re not where we want to be. There’s nine weeks left in the season. Let’s use this as fuel.’

Sports.title: Scottie Scheffler helps Sam Burns in bid to derail Rory McIlroy's Masters defence
Sports.content:
Scottie Scheffler helps Sam Burns in bid to derail Rory McIlroy's Masters defence

Sam Burns enjoyed protein snacks made by Scottie Scheffler's chef during the third round of the Masters at Augusta National as he chases the Green Jacket held by Rory McIlroy

View 2 Images Sam Burns was fuelled by the Scheffler's snack during the Masters

Sam Burns was spotted tucking into protein snacks made by Scottie Scheffler's personal chef as a mid-round treat at Augusta National. Burns played alongside defending champion Rory McIlroy during the third round of the 90th Masters, with his eyes firmly set on the trophy and a £3.5 million payday.

‌



The 29-year-old is making just his fifth Masters appearance in 2026, having featured at the Tour Championship in each of the past five years, while also finishing runner-up at the Canadian Open. Now firmly in contention at Augusta National, he's also been carrying a World No. 1-approved snack in his bag.

‌



"Caroline [Burns' wife] showed up to the house the other day after going to Schefflers," Burns told CBS presenter Amanda Balionis, explaining his unusual mid-round snack choice. "She said 'the Scheffs made you some protein balls,' and I said 'OK, I'll take 'em.'"

‌



Burns carded a one-under 71 on Friday and had already picked up two birdies on the day while playing alongside the world No. 2. "It's fun, right?" he said, reflecting on his position near the top of the leaderboard.

Masters champion refuses to leave Augusta National after missing the cut READ MORE :

"This is what we work so hard for, and this is what we try to prepare for. So at the end of the day, it's fun. Whatever happens is going to happen, so just go out there and enjoy it and play my best."

Burns has also represented the United States in the previous two Ryder and Presidents Cups, though he slipped down the leaderboard on day three as 2026 Players Champion Cameron Young surged into a tie for second place. "I probably won't change much," Young admitted after the second round.

‌



"I think it's so dependent on where you are, what the wind is doing. I think there are certain winds where you can use slopes more easily and they kind of have some bumpers out there, and there's winds where you don't have any.

View 2 Images Sam Burns is playing alongside Rory McIlroy at the Masters

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



"So I think it just depends on hole to hole, what number you get if I can hit something hard and up in the air or if I can't.

"It might end up looking like I am or I'm not when in reality I'm kind of just trying to make the same decisions that I would have today from those places."

Despite fierce competition from the world's finest players, McIlroy remains firmly in front, edging ever closer to a second Green Jacket. "I'll probably try to keep my mind off of it," McIlroy admitted, in reference to his late tee time.

Article continues below

"That distraction is usually a good thing for me, especially with a late tee time and the lead. There's actually two really good semifinals at Monte Carlo in the tennis. So I'll watch that... We've been watching the tennis early in the mornings. So I'll do that."

Sports.title: Bryson DeChambeau's miserable Masters - 'Baptised in lemon juice'
Sports.content:
Bryson DeChambeau's miserable Masters - 'Baptised in lemon juice'

Bryson DeChambeau arrived at Augusta National with high hopes of slipping on the Green Jacket, but he will not play the weekend after a miserable two days at the Masters

View 2 Images Bryson DeChambeau failed to live up to his high expectations at the Masters (Image: Andrew Redington/Getty Images)

What they say about Southern hospitality is true, and you won’t find a warmer welcome than from the people you meet in Augusta, Georgia, this week.

‌



The little tales they tell are delightful, as are the tickling turns of phrase unique to this part of the world. One, in particular, amused me more than the rest. “They look like they been baptised in lemon juice,” Kenny the shuttle driver quipped as we chewed the fat on the buggy ride from the media centre to the golf course to catch the closing stages of Rory McIlroy’s sensational second round.

‌



Those words took hold in the back of my mind for a short while until Bryson DeChambeau made a triple bogey at the last to miss the cut by two.

‌



Scottie Scheffler delivers resounding response after criticism of Masters 'attitude' READ MORE :

Masters champion refuses to leave Augusta National after missing the cut READ MORE :

His sour face after a mystifying and miserable two days will be one of the enduring images of the week. The idiosyncratic, big-hitting American pitched up with such high hopes, feeling ready to exorcise the demons of 12 months ago when he wilted in the final round, unable to match McIlroy’s perseverance.

The 32-year-old had won two LIV Golf events in succession, and he started the week stating his desire to reignite his rivalry with McIlroy and “beat the living you-know-what out of him.”

Thirty-six holes later, he has lost to the Northern Irishman by an astonishing 18 shots and was on an early flight home.

‌



In many markets, DeChambeau was backed into third favorite ahead of McIlroy, but the 36-year-old’s 67-65 start quickly made a mockery of the odds.

For all the latest news and views from The Masters at Augusta National, visit The Mirror US.

View 2 Images No one has was a match for Rory McIlroy in the opening two rounds, but DeChambeau finished a stunning 18 shots adrift (Image: Ben Jared/PGA TOUR via Getty Images)

‌



It was reminiscent of the US Open at Congressional, the scene of his first major triumph 15 years ago, when he blew away the field. It remains to be seen whether he will repeat the feat on Sunday.

But what is already known is that DeChambeau has a longstanding issue to solve if he wants to win around here.

He contended last year despite his woeful iron play from Augusta National’s sloping lies, thanks to some short-game brilliance, but he could not save himself this time.

‌



Golf Channel pundit Brandel Chamblee, fond of sticking the boot into those who defected to LIV, dubbed DeChambeau’s play from the fairway this week as “abysmal.”

His bunker game needs some work, too. Two triple bogeys cost him tee times this weekend, and both were the result of taking multiple shots to escape from the sand.

Bob MacIntyre's excuse for Masters meltdown becomes clear after risking Augusta National wrath READ MORE :

Jon Rahm row breaks out at the Masters as LIV Golf star snaps back READ MORE :

Baffled and bemused throughout his two laps of this great course, his face tightened once more in disgust as he made a pig’s ear of the 18th hole on Friday, where he could have made the cut with a bogey.

‌



McIlroy was a few groups back, going on a run of six birdies in seven holes that had the usually cordial patrons on their feet and chanting his name.

Golf is desperate for an enduring rivalry to define this era. McIlroy and world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler have seldom been in contention at the same time, and the latter might lack the charisma to be the face of the sport.

McIlroy and DeChambeau teased us with their battle at Pinehurst No. 2 in 2024, when DeChambeau emerged victorious, before the American failed to show up for the final-pairing showdown here a year ago.

Article continues below

DeChambeau is eager to fuel the mano-a-mano narrative, but right now, McIlroy is his master.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury's daughter Venezuela attends fight with fiancé 'weeks before wedding'
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury's daughter Venezuela attends fight with fiancé 'weeks before wedding'

Tyson Fury is taking on Arslanbek Makhmudov tonight and his daughter Venezuela will be ringside with fiance Noah Price and her mum Paris

View 3 Images Venezuela Fury with fiance Noah Price (left) and Paris Fury (right)

Tyson Fury's daughter Venezuela will be ringside tonight with her fiance to watch her dad's comeback fight.

‌



Fury is returning to the ring after a 16-month hiatus following his two defeats by Oleksandr Usyk in 2024. He will take on giant Russian Arslanbek Makhmudov at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and will be roared on by several members of his family, including wife Paris, who was fiercely opposed to her husband returning to the ring.

‌



Paris arrived with son Prince John James, daughter Venezuela and her fiance Noah Price who are due to marry in the coming months. Paris said this week: “I’m happy for him. It’s what he wanted, and I knew it’s what he wanted.

‌



3 View 3 Images Venezuela Fury and Noah Price 3 View 3 Images Venezuela Fury, Paris Fury and Prince John James

“All this time, when he kept saying he was out the ring, ‘I’m out the ring, I’m not boxing, I’m not boxing’ – I knew in the back of my mind that wouldn’t be true.” The couple’s eldest daughter, Venezuela, said: “I don’t think he ever retired.”

Paris explained how she tried to encourage Tyson to pursue other interests and said: “I kept suggesting to him, ‘why don’t you train people as a boxer? Why don’t you get involved in something that you enjoy?’. He doesn’t have any hobbies. And it’s hard to take away someone’s life’s passion, and I couldn’t be the one to do it.

‌



“I said to him so many times like, ‘oh, I wish you’d stop boxing now, you’ve done everything you need to do. You don’t need to do it anymore’. But he felt that itch, and he still wants to do it. So I’m not going to deny him that dream.

“He couldn’t find anything else good. No matter what we did, we couldn’t find him something he enjoyed. It’s hard. It’s hard work, a one-track mind with him.”

Tyson Fury's ordinary life outside of boxing and new home on tiny island READ MORE :

Tyson Fury's strict rules for daughter Venezuela before her engagement READ MORE :

Fury revealed this week he had offered his future son-in-law marriage advice when he was nervously asked for permission to tie the knot with his daughter. Fury was paid a visit by amateur boxer Noah after he got engaged to Venezuela in September and the former world heavyweight champion gave his approval – but only after a man to man chat.

Article continues below

“He did ask for my permission. He came in and sat down and I explained that marriage is not an easy thing and they are only young kids,” Fury said. “I asked if this is what they really want? He said yes and I gave him my blessing. Fair play, he wasn’t shaking but I could tell he was nervous. Fair play to him.

“He’s a heavyweight boxer and they say that a daughter always goes for someone like her dad and she definitely has! I don’t know if he’s had a stag do yet – if he does, I’ll be there and I’ll bring the strippers.” A date has yet to be revealed for the wedding and Fury has left all the planning to his wife Paris while he focusednon his comeback fight against Makhmudov.

“I’m looking forward to it, but that will have to wait until after Saturday night,” Fury said. “Fair play to Paris and Venezuela, they’ve actually done this wedding without my input at all. I’ve had zero to do with it. I’m away doing business. I’m not thinking about domestic stuff at home. I’m thinking about the fight and that’s it. I’m out of bounds. Don’t tell me about anything like that.”

Sports.title: Scottie Scheffler delivers resounding response after criticism of Masters 'attitude'
Sports.content:
Scottie Scheffler delivers resounding response after criticism of Masters 'attitude'

Scottie Scheffler was accused of not showing 'a ton of accountability,' and his attitude was called into question after a poor second round at the Masters, but the world No. 1 mustered a firm response

View Image Scottie Scheffler has bounced back after a slow start at the Masters (Image: Maddie Meyer/Getty Images)

Scottie Scheffler was criticized for his "attitude" and a lack of "accountability" after his sluggish start to the Masters, but the world No. 1 fired back in style with a sensational opening to his third round.

‌



Four-time major champion Scheffler was a whopping 12 shots off the lead at the start of play on Saturday, but he tamed Augusta National's front nine with three birdies and an eagle to give himself a chance of contending over his final 27 holes.

‌



Scheffler has made a disappointing start to the season by his high standards. He won The American Express in January, but he did not finish in the top 10 in any of his three starts before the Masters.

‌



Jon Rahm row breaks out at the Masters as LIV Golf star snaps back READ MORE :

And after a two-over-par 74 on Saturday to fall to even par for the tournament, his demeanor on the course was criticised by two-time PGA Tour winner and CBS pundit Matt Every.

"I think the attitude's been poor this year from Scottie," he said. "Yesterday, he striped it around this place and he did not get a lot out of it.

"He had probably three or four lip-outs inside 8-10 feet that could have fallen in, and that number could have been a little better. An easy opportunity for him to look frustrated.

‌



For all the latest news and views from The Masters at Augusta National, visit The Mirror US.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

"Scottie, a lot of times when things go south or maybe he gets a bad break or a lip out, he kind of looks over at [caddie] Ted [Scott] and there's, I don't know... There's just not a ton of accountability there all the time. I feel like I've seen a lot more of that yesterday."

‌



Scheffler said his score on Friday was not reflective of how he played. He told reporters: "I felt like was really challenging. I played really pretty well. I got very, very difficult late in the day yesterday. Then today I felt like I played a lot better than my score.

"I got off to a slow start. A few up-and-downs early that I should have had, but I didn't convert. Then I fought back to get it to even through 12 holes.

Masters champion refuses to leave Augusta National after missing the cut READ MORE :

Bob MacIntyre's excuse for Masters meltdown becomes clear after risking Augusta National wrath READ MORE :

"And then the fairway on 13, probably my only shot that I would rather be able to hit again [after it landed in Rae's Creek]. Maybe a different decision there. That's a tough shot, but I felt like I could make something happen to that pin."

Article continues below

He continued: "I would like to hole a few more putts. I felt like it was rolling nice today, but balls just weren't dropping. Maybe my reads were a little bit off.

"I felt like I was starting on line, could have been the speed on a couple of putts, but overall today I felt like I definitely played better than my score."

Sports.title: Masters champion refuses to leave Augusta National after missing the cut
Sports.content:
Masters champion refuses to leave Augusta National after missing the cut

Two-time Masters champion Jose Maria Olazabal decided to remain at Augusta National to work on his game despite missing the cut at the 2026 Masters after leading early in the first round

View 2 Images Jose Maria Olazabal stuck around after Augusta after failing to make the cut at the Masters (Image: Jared C. Tilton, Getty Images)

Jose Maria Olazabal chose to remain at Augusta to practise on Saturday despite failing to make the cut at the Masters. After opening strongly with a five-under 67 to share the first round lead, Rory McIlroy produced a scintillating second round at The Masters.

‌



The defending champion posted a seven-under 65 to reach 12-under and hold a six-shot advantage in the clubhouse. Olazabal made a strong start on Thursday, but the Spaniard ultimately failed to make the cut despite sidestepping a potential rules breach during his opening round following a contentious 'illegal swing' incident.

‌



Olazabal claimed the Green Jacket in both 1994 and 1999. After securing his first title aged 28, he completed a remarkable recovery from serious injury by capturing another Green Jacket five years later.

‌



However, Olazabal struggled over the opening two days. He finished the first round with two bogeys and a double-bogey after leading early, then posted a 7-over 79 to finish at 9-over and miss the cut.

Masters LIVE: Flying Rory McIlroy closing in on glory as PGA Tour star risks Augusta wrath READ MORE :

Jon Rahm row breaks out at the Masters as LIV Golf star snaps back READ MORE :

After his disappointing performance, Olazabal will not compete through the weekend. But the two-time champion was in no hurry to depart, instead remaining at Augusta to work on his short game, sharpening his skills for his next tournament after acknowledging his frustration.

Speaking after his opening round, Olazabal made certain to enjoy his fleeting moment atop the leaderboard. The 60 year old told reporters on Thursday: "I look at the leaderboard, I saw myself 2-under par, and for a little while I said to myself, hey, I'm leading the Masters. There you go.

‌



"You know, it's one of those things, yeah. Obviously, it was fun."

View 2 Images Olazabal is a two-time Masters winner but faded quickly in the 2026 edition

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



He was satisfied with his initial 18 holes before his form dipped in the second round. Olazabal said: "Well, I've been playing this golf course 37 years. You know, that helps, to be honest.

"You know, my short game was really nice today. It has to be in order to put a decent score, because I'm going to miss a lot of greens hitting woods onto the greens. As hard as the greens are, I know I'm going to miss a lot of greens."

"So, first of all, you have to think about what will be the best side to miss, which side will give you the best chances to up-and-down, and you play from there."

Article continues below

He added: "It was a good round. I mean, I'm pretty happy with it. If somebody would have told me I was going to shoot 2-over par at the beginning of the week the first round, I would have take it."

Sports.title: Grand National fans convinced they've found winner of 'biggest ever' £100,000 bet
Sports.content:
Grand National fans convinced they've found winner of 'biggest ever' £100,000 bet

Racing fans have turned detective to find the winner of the extraordinary £100,000 stake at the Grand National

View 2 Images The winning team: Willie Mullins, Paul Townend and JP McManus (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Fans of horse racing are convinced they know who is behind a £100,000 punt on I Am Maximus ahead of its victory at the Grand National today.

‌



Bookmaker Johnny Dineen revealed on ITV that someone had put down £100,000 on I Am Maximus at 8-1. The horse won the National in 2024 and finished as runner-up in last year's race.

‌



However, this year, the Willie Mullins-trained horse won the punter an incredible £800,000 profit by claiming victory, with Paul Townend riding the horse to victory.

‌



Speaking on ITV prior to the race, Dineen admitted it was the biggest bet he has ever laid. He said: "We’ve laid a whopping bet on I Am Maximus, and it’s the biggest bet we’ve ever laid by a mile."

It left betting ring presenter Brian Gleeson shocked, and he replied: "Oh my God."

View 2 Images Jockey Paul Townend celebrates winning the Grand National on I Am Maximus (Image: Liverpool Echo)

‌



Grand National results LIVE: Full finishers as I Am Maximus wins at Aintree but jockey hospitalised READ MORE :

Grand National jockey banned for not pulling up tired horse before last fence fall READ MORE :

Some racing fans think the extraordinary bet was put on the JP McManus-owned horse by the owner himself.

“Hearing it was JP McManus that put it on. They made it out like an ordinary raceday goer put it on," one person wrote on X.

Another said: “Spare change for JP McManus. He’d probably of had 10x that on, if someone would take the bet.”

‌



Asked if he had bet on the winner, McManus said he "had a little on" I Am Maximus.

If correct, the bet could mean that McManus took home over £1 million in just one day, as the winner of the National reveives £500,000 split between the owner, jockey, trainer and other connections.

The 10-year-old horse looked to have the potential of becoming a Liverpool great when first winning the world’s most famous steeplechase in 2024 – and while he found stablemate Nick Rockett too strong 12 months ago, he returned as the 9-2 favourite to become the first horse since Ginger McCain’s superstar to regain the National crown.

Article continues below

With incidents aplenty taking place around him, I Am Maximus was not always foot-perfect in the hands of Townend, but slowly but surely he stealthily moved into contention and there was an inevitably about the result when he went in pursuit of the bold-jumping Jordans approaching the elbow.

He found plenty to run down the leader and gallop to glory once again, a result which sees McManus become the most successful owner in National history with four victories, while trainer Willie Mullins was also winning the race for a fourth time, putting him alongside George Dockeray, who trained the first ever winner, Lottery, in 1839, Fred Rimell and McCain as the joint record holder.

Sports.title: Bob MacIntyre's excuse for Masters meltdown becomes clear after risking Augusta National wrath
Sports.content:
Bob MacIntyre's excuse for Masters meltdown becomes clear after risking Augusta National wrath

Bob MacIntyre endured an awful week at Augusta National, carding a first-round 80 to blow his chances of contending, and all eyes were on his behaviour as he failed to hide his emotions

Bob MacIntyre was close to withdrawing from the Masters due to an injury after a nightmare week at Augusta National for the Scot.

‌



The 29-year-old was in a foul mood after an eight-over-par 80 to open the tournament, wrecking his hopes of playing the weekend. Amid the frustration, MacIntyre flashed his middle finger in the direction of the 15th green after making a quadruple bogey, and he was reprimanded by Augusta National officials.

‌



He risked stoking further wrath from the club on Friday after carding a one-under-par 71 to miss the cut by three. MacIntyre skipped speaking to members of the media and headed home, but he did vent some frustration on social media.

‌



Jon Rahm row breaks out at the Masters as LIV Golf star snaps back READ MORE :

An AI-generated image depicting him as a Masters gnome — a coveted limited edition ware sold in the gift shop — raising its middle finger appeared on his Instagram page, leaving many feeling he ought to be careful not to create a bad reputation at the home of the first major of the year.

According to The Scotsman, MacIntyre sustained a neck injury earlier this week while working out in the Player Services Building gym. He did not play a practice round on Tuesday, and he pulled out midway through the Par 3 Contest as a result.

It would go some way to explaining MacIntyre's disastrous opening round and the emotions he exuded. The discomfort almost led him to withdraw from the tournament ahead of Friday's second round, but he played through the pain and missed the cut by three shots.

‌



For all the latest news and views from The Masters at Augusta National, visit The Mirror US.

View 2 Images Bob MacIntyre was in a foul mood after a dismal day at Augusta National (Image: ESPN/Augusta National)

It has been a deeply frustrating week for MacIntyre, who had his momentum hindered by a weather delay at the Valero Texas Open seven days ago. He needed to play his final 30 holes on Sunday, and he let slip the chance to claim his third PGA Tour win; JJ Spaun was the man to profit.

‌



MacIntyre's spiky behaviour and bad language on the golf course have been a big talking point of late, but he insisted earlier this week that he will not be changing his personality.

“I know I am volatile and I know the bad language and stuff, but that’s just me," he said. “Even having a little one myself and knowing there are little ones around, I’m not going to change.

View 2 Images MacIntyre drew more attention to himself with his social media post

Article continues below

“I am trying to do my best out on the golf course. I’m a sportsman and it is live sport. I’m going to react the way I want to react. I’m not going to change how I react because there is someone standing there or elsewhere.

“I am trying to do the best that I can and I will take my time after to go and sign autographs with kids and what not, but, when I am playing golf I am red-lining.”

Sports.title: Grand National jockey banned for not pulling up tired horse before last fence fall
Sports.content:
Grand National jockey banned for not pulling up tired horse before last fence fall

Toby McCain-Mitchell, grandson of legendary Red Rum trainer Ginger McCain, was having his first ride in the race on Top Of The Bill who was later under veterinary care

View 2 Images Toby McCain-Mitchell: banned for ten days (Image: GROSSICK PHOTOGRAPHY The Steadings Rockhallhead Collin DG1 4JW 07712577337 www.grossick.co.uk)

A Grand National jockey was banned for ten days after he failed to pull up a tired horse before it fell at the last fence of the big race on Saturday.

‌



Toby McCain-Mitchell, grandson of legendary Red Rum trainer Ginger McCain, was making his debut in the race.

‌



For good luck the 24-year-old carried a lock of three-time race winner Red Rum’s hair in his gloves.

‌



His mount Top Of The Bill, trained by father and son Nigel and Willie Twiston-Davies, was a 50-1 chance for the Aintree feature having recorded a win and a second on his three starts under his young rider this season.

Updates issued on Top Of The Bill and Quai De Bourbon after Grand National falls READ MORE :

Grand National punter bags just shy of £1MILLION after I Am Maximus wins Aintree race READ MORE :

He was right up with the leaders during the first half of the race, holding second place jumping the Chair before going to the front at the 20th of the 30 fences.

‌



However he made a mistake at the 25th obstacle, Valentines, on the second circuit, from where he began to gradually fall back through the field and was right out of the reckoning by the time he fell at the last fence.

Top of The Bill was one of three horses to require veterinary treatment. He was assessed on the racecourse by the Aintree team and was walked back to the stables for further monitoring.

View 2 Images Top of the Bill ridden by Toby McCain-Mitchell, front, clears a fence during the Grand National horse race at Aintree racecourse in Liverpool, Saturday, April 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Jon Super)

Article continues below

Two other fallers, Quai De Bourbon and Mr Vango were taken by horse ambulance, back to the stables to be assessed by vets. All remaining horses were accounted for.

The Aintree stewards held an inquiry to consider whether McCain-Mitchell should have pulled up Top Of The Bill “having been in a prominent position before weakening rapidly”

The report said: “The rider and the Veterinary Officer were interviewed and recordings of the incident were viewed. Having considered the evidence, McCain-Mitchell was suspended for 10 days for failing to pull up when the horse had tailed off.”
